title: The Confession of Thomas
subtitle: Selected passages from the Gospel of John
source: Text drawn from the King James Version (1611, public domain). Editorial framing by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: Let us also go
sections.framing: Thomas appears three times in John's Gospel, and each time the evangelist gives him a sentence that has been remembered ever since. The first comes when word reaches the Lord that Lazarus has died, and he turns to go back into Judaea, where the authorities have lately tried to stone him. The disciples shrink from the road. Thomas does not argue and does not boast; he proposes only that if the Master is going to his death, they had better not be left behind.
paragraphs: Then said Jesus unto them plainly, Lazarus is dead.
And I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, to the intent ye may believe; nevertheless let us go unto him.
Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples, Let us also go, that we may die with him.
notes: Didymus is the Greek for Thomas's Aramaic name; both words mean 'twin.' The tradition does not record who his twin was.
St. John Chrysostom reads the line as the first stirring of the martyr's courage Thomas would later show in India.

sections.title: Lord, we know not whither thou goest
sections.framing: In the upper room, when the Lord begins the farewell discourse and tells his disciples that he is going to prepare a place for them and that they know the way, it is Thomas who speaks up for the puzzled silence of the others. His question is the question of every disciple who has been told something deeper than he can yet hold. And it draws from the Lord one of the great I Am sayings of the Fourth Gospel.
paragraphs: Thomas saith unto him, Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
notes: Thomas's honesty serves the whole Church: the question that he was unafraid to ask gives every later reader the answer.

sections.title: My Lord and my God
sections.framing: The third and most famous scene comes a week after the Resurrection. On the first Sunday Thomas had not been with the disciples when the Lord came in through the closed doors; on hearing the report he refused belief and named the test he would require. Eight days later the Lord came again, and offered him exactly what he had asked. The Fathers note that the apostle does not in fact stretch out his hand. He sees, and he confesses; and the confession is the highest the New Testament records from any human mouth.
paragraphs: And after eight days again his disciples were within, and Thomas with them: then came Jesus, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst, and said, Peace be unto you.
Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
notes: The Sunday on which the Orthodox Church reads this passage is called Thomas Sunday, the Antipascha, the eighth day on which the Lord returned. Thomas's doubt is read not as a failure but as the providence by which the Resurrection was tested and certified for every later believer.

'My Lord and my God' is the only place in the Gospels where Christ is addressed as God by one of the Twelve and the address is received without correction. The Fathers from St. Cyril of Alexandria onward treat it as a foundation text for the divinity of the Son.
